nameStory: The 'Humped' Trashline Orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive rounded bump on its abdomen that looks like a tiny camel's hump. Like other trashline orbweavers, it decorates its web with a vertical line of debris - bits of leaves, prey remains, and other 'trash' - creating what looks like nature's own recycling project. This clever camouflage helps the spider blend in with its cluttered web decoration.
description: The Humped Trashline Orbweaver is a small, chunky spider with a characteristic rounded hump on the back of its abdomen. Its body is typically brownish or grayish, perfectly matching the debris it collects in its web. These spiders are quite small, with females reaching only about 1/4 to 1/3 inch in body length. What makes them truly special is their habit of building vertical 'trashlines' in their otherwise classic circular orb webs.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for a classic circular orb web with a distinctive vertical line of debris running through the center - bits of leaves, insect remains, and plant material that feel dry and crumbly to the touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small, compact spider with a rounded hump on the back of the abdomen that you can clearly see in profile, giving it an almost turtle-like silhouette

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Mottled brown and gray coloration with subtle patterns that help it blend seamlessly with the debris in its web - often appearing almost dusty or weathered

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Quite small with females measuring about 1/4 to 1/3 inch in body length, roughly the size of a small button or pencil eraser

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often positions itself along the trashline in its web, remaining motionless and nearly invisible among the collected debris

habitat: Found in gardens, woodlands, and forest edges throughout New England, particularly in areas with plenty of vegetation that provides debris for web decoration. They prefer spots with some protection from wind, often building webs between shrubs, in tall grass, or along woodland paths where falling leaves and plant matter naturally accumulate.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders emerge and begin building their first webs, often with smaller, less elaborate trashlines as they're still learning their craft.
seasonality.summer: Peak web-building season when mature females create the most impressive trashline decorations, taking advantage of abundant insects and plant debris.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and females may be seen with egg sacs, while their webs become particularly noticeable as vegetation dies back around them.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures, but eggs overwinter in protected locations, ready to hatch the following spring.

funFact: This spider is essentially an artist and architect rolled into one - it carefully selects and arranges debris in its web not just for camouflage, but the trashline may also make the web more visible to birds, preventing them from accidentally flying through and destroying it!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Conical Trashline Orbweaver, but the Humped species has a rounded bump on its abdomen while the Conical has a pointed, cone-shaped projection. Memory trick: 'Humped has a hump, Conical has a cone' - look at the silhouette from the side to tell them apart.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'trashline' might sound derogatory, but it's actually a technical term that reflects these spiders' remarkable recycling behavior - they're essentially nature's first environmental artists, turning waste into functional art.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative, the Conical Trashline Orbweaver, the Humped species has a distinctly rounded abdominal projection rather than a sharp, pointed one. Both species create similar trashline webs, but the body shape difference is quite clear when viewed from the side. The Humped Trashline Orbweaver also tends to be slightly smaller and more compact overall than its conical cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Conical Trashline Orbweaver differs from its close relative, the Humped Trashline Orbweaver, primarily in the shape of its abdominal projection—conical and pointed rather than rounded and humped.
